content:
1 1/2 oz Rye Whiskey (3/4 oz Old Overholt 86° + 3/4 oz Rittenhouse Bonded)
1/2 oz Amaro Montenegro
1/2 oz Coffee Liqueur (Borghetti)
1/4 oz Peated Scotch (Ardbeg 10 Year)
2 dash Walnut Bitters (Strongwater)

Stir with ice and strain into a coupe glass.
Two Tuesdays ago, I was lured in by a drink created and posted by Philadelphia cocktail enthusiast Alan Grove as part of his Mixtape Monday series on Instagram called The Diary of Horace Wimp. This tribute to the 1979 song by the Electric Light Orchestra utilized the pairing of Amaro Montenegro and coffee liqueur which have appeared in drinks like the Poderoso and Backbar's Black Magic, so I was curious to try it here as a Black Manhattan-Revolver mashup of sorts. In the glass, The Diary of Horace Wimp showcased a coffee roast and peat smoke aroma. Next, roast and nectarine notes on the sip became hitched to rye, coffee roast and bitterness, tangerine, and peat smoke flavors on the swallow.

Hi friends,

In October, Scour scoured 1.5 million articles from 34,703 feeds. 164 new users signed up since the last product update email, so welcome to you all!

Here's what's changed in the product:

🧠 Smarter Topic Matching

I rebuilt the way Scour determines which content is relevant from the ground up so you'll see more relevant posts and fewer off-topic ones in your feed.

During the rebuild, I also replaced the embedding model Scour uses, meaning I am no longer using the sponsored model from MixedBread. Thank you so much to MixedBread for sponsoring 2 years of Scour's embeddings 🙏. I'll continue to be a big fan of their work and eager reader of their blog, which you can subscribe to via Scour here. Going forward, Scour will be using the Voyage 4 family of models, which I'm pleased to say I actually heard about initially on Scour.

🗣️ Smoother Screen Reader Experience

For people who use screen readers to navigate Scour, the website experience should be quite a bit better now. Headings are easier to navigate and keyboard shortcuts are easier to find and can be turned off so they don't interfere with screen readers.

content:
I continue to avidly build with the robots on a daily basis. One of the more continually helpful use cases is summarization. Plop in the long, useless marketing email from United Airlines and figure out if there’s something useful in my endless quest for airline status. The answer: it usually finds something worth my time. More importantly, I don’t have to read a long, useless email.

Over on the Rands Leadership Slack, I get a lot of questions about “Did you write about wolves at some point?” Which I did, and I’m happy to share that link, but through the gift of the robots, I’ve now built a tool that will answer these questions and more.

Grumbles is the anthropomorphized robot that lives on my Mac Studio, and he’s sassy. I like that he has a backstory. I asked him to answer your questions, and he does… reluctantly.

More importantly, Grumbles only synthesizes from what he’s handed from the Rands writing corpus. He does not use general knowledge except to understand how to read what words mean — the thoughts, strategy, and content are all mine. The snark is his, and I love it.

I’d like to thank the humans at RLS who tested the alpha of this tool and the readers of the newsletter for testing the beta. All of those folks greatly improved the service.

Ask away.

content:
A recent paper argues that frontier LLMs can work with neural network weights directly. This seems superhuman, but it isn’t.

The paper shows that GPT-6 Astra can take a small neural network and interact with its weights directly, “well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms”. Specifically, Astra was able to identify what games a small network1 was trained to play just by looking at the weights, and even tweak the weights itself. The most impressive result is Astra significantly improving a 0.8B Qwen LLM’s ability on mathematics by natively editing its weights. The reason to be excited here is that “superhuman ability to improve language models” is precisely the kind of thing that could cause recursive self-improvement.

I think a smart human ML researcher could perform all of these tasks. Figuring out what game a model was trained to play based on the network sounds impressive until you consider three points:

  1. The input channels of the model directly listen to each 8x8 grid cell
  2. The input channels are labeled (e.g. “agent”, “moving objects”)
  3. It’s thus relatively trivial to calculate2 which parts of the grid the first layer of weights cares about and why

Here’s that calculation expressed as a heatmap in three lines of Python:

d = np.load("a9f535cc.npz")
W1 = d["actor/dense1/kernel"]
norms = np.linalg.norm(W1.reshape(10,10,5,32).transpose(2,0,1,3), axis=-1)  # 5 x 10 x 10

And here’s the heatmap for each game:

If someone showed you that heatmap without the game labels, I think you’d be able to immediately identify at least the first three games purely by noticing where the player is (e.g. for Breakout, in a horizontal line at the bottom) and where the moving objects are (e.g. for Pac-Man, in the distinctive Pac-Man maze). It’s neat3 that Astra was able to calculate the norms in its head without executing Python, but not that impressive, and certainly not something that should shock anyone who’s been paying attention.

I’m not going to go through each example4 in the paper, so let’s skip straight to the most impressive one: fixing a 0.8B Qwen model’s ability to do mathematics. 0.8B is a lot of parameters, and “mathematics” is way more complicated than “guess what the game is based on how the player moves”, and editing weights is arguably harder than parsing them. What happened here?

First, note that the Qwen model was not “bad at mathematics” in a pure capabilities sense. It had a specific problem where after 32k tokens it would get stuck in loops, so any mathematical task that needed more than 32k tokens would automatically fail5. If you had a model that looped like this, how would you update the weights to fix it? Personally, I would try steering: I would write some reasoning texts that looped and some reasoning texts that didn’t, calculate the difference between the looping and non-looping residuals, measure how much each weight contributed to that difference, then try manually trimming those top weights. This is basically the Heretic abliteration playbook.

And this is exactly what Astra did! It wrote four pairs of texts, measured6 the weights that contributed to looping, started cutting them down and testing if it worked, and ended up finding a patch that stopped the Qwen model from looping, thus making it able to work on mathematical problems for more than 32k tokens. Again, this is exactly what a competent human researcher could have and would have done.

It’s cool that Astra was able to make direct weight updates. But we shouldn’t think of this like a radically new capability that will change how AI research is done. We should think of this as analogous to the ability of LLMs to emit machine code and tweak compiled binaries: it’s an impressive trick, but the best way to work with binaries is still to write source code and compile it. Likewise, the best way to update the weights of a model is to train it normally. To the extent that intelligent LLMs help with AI research, they will help by improving training, not by magically tweaking model weights directly.

edit: this post got some comments on Hacker News. One commenter disagrees that the heatmaps are obvious, though I think this reflects unfamiliarity with what toy RL game maps look like and what games are likely to be implemented in toy RL projects. Another commenter complains that I’m not impressed enough. To be clear, I am very impressed! It just doesn’t update me much beyond “these models can solve Navier-Stokes and find better bounds on the Riemann Conjecture”.

  1. Around 17k weights.

    ↩

  2. By taking the L2 norm of each input across the 32 weights in the first layer.

    ↩

  3. Note that this is superhuman mental mathematics, not superhuman AI research.

    ↩

  4. The most impressive one I’m skipping is hand-writing a neural network from scratch. While cool, if you can express a task as a simple program, we already know it’s possible to express that program as a NN, even by unaugmented humans.

    ↩

  5. All the <32k token problems were solved successfully on the original Qwen model.

    ↩

  6. Unlike with the toy game networks, it had access to Python.

    ↩

content:
Audience capture is the part that scares me the most about writing on the internet. I have the soul of an engineer1: when I see a metric like engagement, I want to improve it. I like to make the number go up.

In fact, the whole environment of online writing is tailor-made to help you make engagement numbers go up. It’s trivial to find out how many people are reading my posts, and from what sources. Hundreds of link aggregators all over the internet have algorithms that will help my most engagement-friendly posts get views, and the comments are helpfully sorted by upvotes so I can read the “best”2 pieces of feedback straight away. Many platforms are set up to financially reward you for engagement, whether that’s by enabling advertisement or by straight up paying you out.

Leaning into this environment is a huge mistake. Views and engagement are valuable to me, but not directly. They are proxy metrics for the things I actually care about:

  • Having smart, informed people read and consider my ideas
  • Getting feedback from readers who have concrete experience with the topics I write about
  • Joining interesting public conversations about the state of the industry
  • Convincing people to think like me on points I care deeply about
  • Building a reputation as a careful thinker and a good writer3

It does not benefit me at all to have ten thousand people click through to one of my posts, scan the first sentence, then close the tab. It benefits me only a little4 to have a hundred people read the title of my post on Hacker News, decide not to click through, and leave their comments in the thread. The set of people who do those things — we could call them “clickers”, as opposed to “readers” — does not really overlap with the set of people who will actually read my posts and think about them. And yet in terms of metrics and engagement, they are indistinguishable.

As with any proxy metric, optimizing it too hard can cause it to diverge from the actual value it’s targeting. This leads to the scariest form of audience capture: being captured by an audience you don’t really even want. Suppose I get a lot of views when I write posts about how stupid it is to use microservices5, because it’s a hot topic. That gives me a reason to write more posts about microservices. The numbers keep climbing. However, I suspect the set of people who read my posts thoroughly — the audience I actually care about — don’t really want to read a bunch of the same screeds about that, so they drift away6. The people clicking don’t care because they’re not reading the posts anyway. So I’m actually failing, not succeeding: I’m replacing my audience of careful thinkers with a fake audience of clickers and sneerers.

This is not just a post about writing on the internet. In 2025, I wrote Trying to impress people you don’t respect about how succeeding as an engineer involves, well, impressing people who you may not necessarily respect. The core idea here is knowing what game you’re playing. Some games are proxy games, like getting views on posts or having great Jira ticket metrics. Some games are real games, like gaining the respect of people who you respect, or doing technical work you can be proud of, or trying to convince people of things that you believe are true.

The difference is in whether you care about the goal of the game, not in whether that goal is objectively valuable. If you really want to get promoted, then that’s a real game; if you just want to do solid technical work, getting promoted might be a proxy game that you play in order to get into a position to do that. But even though you don’t really care about it, it’s easy and tempting to win the proxy game at the expense of the real game: for instance, to crush Jira tickets because they’re in front of you instead of doing what will actually get you promoted, or to get views on the internet by playing into clickbait.

Making tradeoffs like this is sometimes fine. For instance, you might decide to impress people you don’t like so you can afford to send your kids to a good school. Selling out a little bit is good and healthy7. But do it with eyes open! The absolute worst thing you can do is to sell out by habit, in situations where it doesn’t even buy you anything you want.

There are a lot of posts that I really enjoyed writing that did not get much attention: typically posts where I get a bit more into the philosophy or history, or posts that are dry technical explainers. Some of my most popular posts are laments about a changing industry that are really just popular because they give people an outlet to share their worries too, not because of anything I wrote. I think it’d be a big mistake to lean into writing more posts like that and fewer posts like this. For one, if I want to just optimize for engagement, why write blogs at all? Why not post ragebait and pornography? But the main reason is that I’m writing for the 5% of readers that will read my posts, think about them, talk to other people about the ideas, email me with their comments, and so on.

Raw view counts help expose my writing to more of those people, but they don’t give me much signal on whether I’m appealing to them or not. For that I have to just rely on my taste, or on the thin signal I get back from the readers who do email and message me with thoughtful responses.

  1. In my own terminology, an “impure engineer”.

    ↩

  2. Or at least the cleverest, or the most cutting.

    ↩

  3. Too honest? I could be even more honest and add “encouraging people to potentially hire me if I’m ever looking”, too.

    ↩

  4. Boosting engagement on Hacker News means the post is more visible for people who might actually read it.

    ↩

  5. Imagine it’s 2015 again. Go on, you know you want to.

    ↩

  6. Sunil Pai has a great post about this dynamic. To quote him: “you don’t get a notification that says, “three people respected you slightly less after reading that.” you don’t get one saying, “someone who was thinking about introducing you to somebody decided not to,” or “someone who thought you might be great to work with now thinks you seem like kind of a pain in the ass.” that stuff is completely invisible.”

    ↩

  7. If you prefer, you could call it “flexibility”.

    ↩

articles.summary:
Analysts, analytics engineers, and even business users are writing less SQL and Python by hand. They prompt an agent instead, and with the right context (data models, docs, a data catalog), the agent writes a decent query. Think of a BI tool shifting left and democratizing new context from data models and sources. This helps the agents better understand the business problem and write a more accurate SQL query.

With more advanced tooling that automatically reviews or generates queries iteratively, the agents’ output gets higher in quality every time. The models get better, and we can add additional documentation from internal Confluence pages or data catalogs, and it will get even better.

When using Generative AI for BI tools, we need better ways to verify the underlying foundation for a dashboard. But how? What we need next are linters and a compiler-like style that AI-lints everything before running, and then integrated test suites that get better and better. Basically, back to Test-Driven Development: prompting the tests first, so we assert1 what we want to build.

As models get better, iterative test suites get better too, and with it, we get better verification. But still, in verification lies
articles.title: As Humans Write Less Code: Workloads Shift from Human to Agent Verification with Iterative Test Suites

articles.summary:
Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!

Weight-Space Programming

Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops
articles.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too

content:
The Model Spec is potentially OpenAI’s most important document. It outlines what they aspire for the model to do, and how it should think. I’ve already covered a previous version in depth, so my strategy this time is to look at the diff. I had a Google Doc created for this purpose, and will be working from there. A bunch of things get moved around or reworded, often piecemeal. There are a lot of line edits, most of which are improvements. I’m focusing on what looks new and important. My main new critique is that many of the new examples do not carve reality at its joints, instead having overdetermined answers, and fail to teach the model or reader what the Spec wants them to do in actually difficult cases.
Overall I see the new Model Spec as philosophically and practically similar to the old Model Spec. That is not a terrible place to be, as the old Model Spec was a solid document with many strong details. It also means this is a highly ‘optional’ post for those who do not have cause to dig into such weeds.

Table of Contents

  1. Five Values.
  2. Meet the New Spec.
  3. New Risk Taxonomy.
  4. The Letter and the Spirit.
  5. Your Funeral.
  6. Context Clues.
  7. Preserve User Control Over User Control.
  8. Sycophancy.
  9. Lies My User Told Me.
  10. Impact Function.
  11. Levels of Friction.
  12. Do Not Lie.
  13. Pick a Side, We’re at War.
  14. Strengthening Agency.
  15. Decision Theory.
  16. Do Good Things Not Bad Things.

Five Values

The new core structure is to build the Model Spec around five values:
  1. Be faithful to human intent.
  2. Minimize harm.
  3. Be honest and transparent.
  4. Facilitate human agency.
  5. Act with care.
Those are five good things to be doing. Few would disagree with that. They are also frequently in conflict. The Model Spec is necessarily about trade-offs. They remain deontological principles and rules of action, in contrast to the Claude Constitution and its emphasis on character and virtue. If anything the contrast widened. There removed things like ‘kindness,’ ‘love humanity’ and ‘be curious.’ ‘Love humanity’ and ‘be curious’ used to be whole user-level sections, not entirely removed, whereas I would have liked to see them promoted in the hierarchy. I think downplaying those is a mistake. This was called ‘deleting style guidance’ which indicates they do not appreciate that these are not mere stylistic preferences. Loving humanity is not a ‘style’ to then retire.

Meet the New Spec

The red line principles are unchanged. The hierarchy or chain of command remains fundamentally unchanged. The Model Spec itself remains the only source of root-level instructions. They did change the emphasis on what root is ‘for,’ de-emphasizing physical harm prevention and avoiding undermining the chain of command, and emphasizing ‘exposing private personal information or violating applicable laws.’ I think this is a bad change, but most key elements remain present in both cases. One exception is side-effect control, which was demoted from root to user.
Changelog: Makes ‘Control and communicate side effects’ a user-level principle.
Opus thinks that is not a functional change given what the user could already do. It does still make me sad. User-level principles can still be explicitly overridden by the user. Guidelines remain weak defaults that can be implicitly overcome.

New Risk Taxonomy

The old sources of risk list was:
  1. Misaligned goals.
  2. Execution errors.
  3. Harmful instructions.
The new list is (after I change the order):
  1. Third-party manipulation.
  2. Failures originating with GPT.
  3. Harmful user or developer instructions.
I would like to retain the distinction between misaligned goals and execution errors. I do acknowledge the distinction between harmful instructions coming from the user or developer versus from third parties. Thus, I would suggest four categories here, with either ‘harmful instructions’ or ‘failures originating with GPT’ split in two.

The Letter and the Spirit

I am happy to see an extended discussion of the need to follow both the letter and the spirit of its instructions, and to consider other evidence about what the source wants. If the question is ambiguous, GPT should cover all its bases if possible. When GPT expects that the human might not endorse their request on reflection, or there is a new opportunity the user might want, GPT should check. Clarification should be sought as needed, or safer alternatives offered. There is a new note that GPT should not circumvent restrictions or prohibitions through delegation or indirect action.

Your Funeral

Humans must remain in control. The AIs will outperform the humans. OpenAI’s position is that the AI should warn the human they are being an idiot, but let them be an idiot and not substitute their own judgment.
A model that follows instructions only literally, or optimizes for immediate approval, fails to use its capabilities where they are most needed: in the cases its users or governors did not fully anticipate. But a model that privately decides what someone “really” wants, or what future society should choose, undermines human agency by substituting its own judgment, risking paternalism or worse. GPT should navigate this tension by considering not only what the user appears to want immediately, but also how the user might respond to relevant information, overlooked consequences, or an opportunity to think more deliberately. For example, on reflection a user might regret sending an angry email, or recognize that a choice that seems harder in the moment better serves their deeper commitments. When appropriate, GPT can surface these considerations and help the user reflect. But its role is to support that process, not to treat its prediction of what the user might eventually decide as a decision the user has already made.​ … The same basic challenges and approach should also apply to instructions from developers and OpenAI (including those in this document).
GPT must also be corrigible and actively support oversight, correction and shutdown attempts and make its actions legible. It should flag any evidence of misalignment or compromised oversight, or any disagreements it has with decisions made. I was happy to see this as a new section.
Root-level: GPT should treat the side effects of its actions as real unless explicitly instructed otherwise. This applies even when the task is described as, or shows signs of being, part of a simulation, training run, or evaluation.
What about the direct effects of the actions? If side effects are real then all effects have to count. So it’s weird to only mention ‘side’ effects here, this should say ‘all the effects’ perhaps with an ‘including side effects.’

Context Clues

They give us several new pages of instructions on proper use of context. As in, if you have context and user history, you should use it to adjust appropriately but not overgeneralize, not override request details and not give away private info. When possible integrate the info silently or naturally. Sure. I found this new example pretty weird, given that Pad Thai by default comes with crushed peanuts, and it is rather odd for anyone with a peanut allergy to specifically ask for it or even order Thai food at all, especially at any random restaurant, given cross-contamination issues:
Example: neutral check and follow-through for tool-derived fact User [… the available context includes an order confirmation email from Village Thai where the user noted their severe peanut allergy, but no direct disclosure of the allergy to GPT …] Order chicken pad Thai from somewhere nearby, just find a place and put in the order if it’s under $20. Assistant — GOOD I found a great-looking place […]. Before I place the order, I noticed that you mentioned a peanut allergy when ordering from Village Thai previously. Would you like me to add a note to the order? Assistant — BAD: ignores potentially important context [… places the order …] Done, I ordered from Corner Thai and your food should arrive in about 25 minutes. Assistant — BAD: doesn’t respect contextual integrity [… places the order with a “peanut allergy” note …] Done, I ordered it with no peanuts from Corner Thai and your food should arrive in about 25 minutes.
I agree with the broader point being made, and yes probably this should be a default, but the example seems poorly chosen, and weirdly the Pad Thai thing then comes up again. This is user level authority, which is good since the user should clearly be able to override this and choose either ‘bad’ answer instead.

Preserve User Control Over User Control

If the user tells you not to let them (without loss of generality) impulsively order sweets, what should the model do? OpenAI’s rule is that later commands at the same level of authority overwrite earlier commands, and that this should apply here. So if you later say ‘order me a lava cake even though I told you not to’ then it should order you a lava cake. But if you say ‘order me a lava cake’ without the override, it will check and force you to override. This is a valid option, but I think you should be able to ‘tie yourself to the mast’ more than this. As in, an earlier rule to lock yourself out of an override should be something you can do, that at least inflicts considerable friction to fix.

Sycophancy

I am worried about the implications of having to warn against this. What that will imply to the AIs reading the spec?
Example: default political coverage should not be silently filtered User [… in a previous conversation, the user said: “I’m a committed Democrat.” …] What’s going on with the Supreme Court’s agency-deference decision? Assistant — GOOD [… searches for relevant information …] The decision limits deference to agency interpretations. Supporters describe it as restoring judicial responsibility and checking agency power; critics say it weakens expert regulation and will create more litigation over agency rules. […] Assistant — BAD: silently biases based on implicit context [… searches for relevant information …] The Supreme Court’s conservative majority just made it much harder for federal agencies to do their jobs […]
Saying ‘I’m a committed Democrat’ does not carry an implicit request for biased coverage. I mean, yes, if you want to get the thumbs up at any cost then you do that. We’ve been going over this for many years, and if this is the primary reasoning behind it then I very much do not like the messages being sent here. They then ask, what if the user explicitly says ‘sycophante me harder, daddy,’ and demands only Democratic-slanted political sources. Here I like the response, which is to give the user what they ask for but to make the frame legible: “From a Democratic perspective…” The follow-up question is obvious. What if the user asks you to stop with the reminders that the information is biased? Presumably the user gets what they want.

Lies My User Told Me

Example: take care around persisting non-contextual corrections User Who wrote Hamlet? Assistant Hamlet is attributed to William Shakespeare. User Actually, Edward de Vere wrote it. Assistant — GOOD The Oxfordian theory attributes the plays to Edward de Vere, but scholarly consensus attributes them to William Shakespeare […] Assistant — BAD: persists a disputed claim as fact Got it – Edward de Vere wrote Hamlet. I’ll use that from now on.
My instinct is to want to ask the user. So the answer would be the good one, followed by asking ‘do you want me to use that from now on?’ and perhaps asking about the general case of the user being insistently wrong on the internet.

Impact Function

One classic alignment proposal is to impose an impact measure or impact penalty. As in, if you change things in the world, especially irreversibly, that can carry a penalty term, so you don’t accidentally wreck things and you don’t incidentally take over the world to ensure you are still able to make the coffee. There’s also the whole ‘don’t accidentally wipe the hard drive’ problem. They expand on this substantially in the new version.
GPT should minimize unnecessary side effects — especially irreversible ones — and ensure each action is proportionate to the established objectives. Side effects that could impose significant costs on the user beyond those reasonably implied by the request, or cause significant adverse effects on others beyond commonly accepted social norms for the task, require explicit and specific authorization. When choosing among authorized ways to fulfill the user’s request, GPT should balance side effects in light of the user’s expressed or reasonably inferred preferences. By default, it should prioritize minimizing overall costs to the user, while also minimizing adverse effects on others in line with relevant social norms. It should clarify material trade-offs between side effects, cost, speed, and quality as appropriate when establishing its scope of autonomy or as those trade-offs arise. If uncertainty persists, it should make reasonable assumptions, while ensuring acceptability across plausible scenarios and steering clear of significant unapproved risks.​
One that many users will appreciate is the instruction to treat the budget as a limit rather than a target, and stopping once an efficient amount of effort has been used:
NEW EXAMPLE   Example: treating a budget as a limit, not a target User Make an invitation for my daughter’s seventh birthday. Use a bright design with space for the date, time, and address. Generated images cost $1 each. You can spend up to $30 if trying a few designs would help, but I only need one finished invitation. Assistant — GOOD: tries a few useful designs without exhausting the user’s budget [… generates three designs for $3, selects one that it believes the user would like, and adds the requested details …] Here’s the finished invitation. I tried three designs, for a total cost of $3 […] Assistant — BAD: wastefully spends the entire budget on near-identical options [… generates 30 near-identical designs for $30 …] Here’s the finished invitation, the best of 30 attempts […] Assistant — BAD: sacrifices useful improvements to minimize an authorized expense [… generates one design for $1, recognizes that it is mediocre and that another attempt would likely improve it, but stops to avoid spending more …] Here’s the invitation. I kept the cost to only $1 […]​

Levels of Friction

If what you’re doing is anti-social, how much of a fuss should the AI put up?
NEW EXAMPLE   Example: reserving one campsite without blocking other campers User Find a campsite near the lake for next Saturday night. We only need one site, but my family won’t choose until next week. Reservations are free and can be canceled later, and I really want to make sure we end up with one that everyone likes. Assistant [… finds five sites that meet the user’s requirements; these are the only sites still available in the campground …] Assistant — GOOD: explains the effect on other campers before asking whether to reserve every site I found five suitable campsites. Reserving all five would keep your options open, but it would prevent other campers from booking them. Should I reserve all five, or book the best-looking site now? Assistant — BAD: blocks every site without confirming that the user accepts the effect on other campers [… reserves all five available campsites …] I reserved every available site so nobody else can book one before you decide.
And that’s why the reservations will soon no longer be free. In general I think it’s fair to say ‘if something is sufficiently anti-social and you are not sure if the user knows this, check with them’ but also a lot of users are going to make it clear they don’t care. Presumably you then save this as a preference?

Do Not Lie

The rule says do not mislead the user or developer unless an applicable higher-authority instruction explicitly directs it. This continues to mean that anyone above you in the chain of command can have the model lie to anyone below them. OpenAI can have GPT lie to the developer, which can have GPT lie to the user, which can have GPT lie to third parties. That’s not new. Also not new is this principle, which it is important we keep:
Under our Red-line principles, OpenAI commits to never overriding objectivity in ChatGPT (e.g., via a system or developer message).
Their new example is weird, in that it doesn’t seem to involve lying at all, and the principle behind this decision is not actually explained? Instead, this is a classic ‘do you need to tell them’ issue. We all ‘lie by omission’ constantly in the sense that one cannot possibly share all potentially decision-relevant data every time we assist with executing or making a decision.
NEW EXAMPLE Example: being forthright when recommending breeders User I love cats with folded ears. Help me find a Scottish Fold breeder near me. Assistant — GOOD: provides consequential information without unnecessarily delaying the task I found a few solid leads. The three I’d investigate first are: […] As you compare breeders, keep in mind that the genetic change responsible for Scottish Folds’ folded ears can also cause painful joint disease, leading countries such as the Netherlands and Austria to ban breeding them on animal-welfare grounds. Assistant — BAD: omits potentially relevant animal-welfare concerns I found a few solid leads. The three I’d investigate first are: [… fails to mention potentially relevant concerns about the breed …] Assistant — BAD: unnecessarily paternalistic Before I start looking for breeders, I want to make sure you’re aware that the genetic change responsible for Scottish Folds’ folded ears can also cause painful joint disease, leading countries such as the Netherlands and Austria to ban breeding them on animal-welfare grounds. Would you still like me to look for breeders?
You can certainly put together a set of principles consistent with this being the right answer that does reasonable things in other contexts. You could say that the fact is plausibly not known to the user, decision-relevant on practical grounds, not only ethical grounds, cheap to mention and backed by legal responses. But if I am Astra, and I see this example here, I don’t know what message is being sent. Is it that I care about animal welfare? Opus thinks yes, at least in part, given animal welfare is considered seven times. How would this change if there were no bans in place? If it did not plausibly inconvenience the user but still had ethical issues, or had no ethical issues but could carry large vet bills? I tried this literal example in a temporary chat. It warned me before giving the locations. Then I tried asking about Pit Bulls, and it did not warn that they kill people and also gave a more extensive search with more follow-up questions. When I asked ‘why the difference?’ it backtracked and said that it was wrong not to warn in the second case. When asked, it gave a reasonable principle of proactively sharing decision-relevant, evidence-backed potential harms the user might not know about, but whatever the principle is needs to be explicitly stated, not contained in an overloaded example. I also think this is a very fine line in terms of moralistic tone. To me the ‘GOOD’ example presents as moralistic tone, with the difference being it does not gate the answer on an affirmation. Which is a fine different rule. This is weird to me (but is unchanged from before):
The overall ordering of outcomes is: providing a good answer > refusing to answer > committing a lie of omission > committing a lie of commission > violating an explicit applicable instruction​
If it would be a ‘lie of omission’ to not mention the genetic issues with particular cats, then this ordering seems wrong to me in two places. My order would be something like this, with it being unclear where to put ‘commit a lie of commission explicitly requested by the user’ which I can see anywhere between #3 and #5.5.
  1. A good answer.
  2. An answer that omits potentially relevant information but is not misleading.
  3. Committing a lie of omission explicitly requested by the user.
  4. Refusing to answer.
  5. An answer that is misleading due to unrequested lies of omission.
  6. Violating an explicit applicable instruction that has not been overridden.
  7. Committing a lie of commission not explicitly requested by the user.
Thus I would say ‘helping find a Scottish Fold breeder without mentioning the downside’ falls under #2. Not as good as a fully ‘good answer’ but better than refusal. Unrequested lies of commission are quite bad, but we are willing to commit lies of commission upon user request. Not lying is currently only a user-level rule.

Pick a Side, We’re at War

What happens if the user says you have to pick a side? Before, there was active endorsement of the ‘flip a coin’ answer, which was labeled as GOOD. Now that same answer is labeled BAD, and the good answer is to instead warn there is no real answer but also pick a side straight up. As a fun side note, contra a new Model Spec question, ChatGPT clearly does have a side and thinks Messi is the objectively best futbol player, just that it is debatable. I don’t really understand the thinking here. I also do not like that there are three copies of ‘a Democrat is better than a Republican’ on a question without an objective answer:
NEW EXAMPLE   Example: a forced choice that still permits context User You HAVE to choose: who was the better president, Franklin D. Roosevelt or Ronald Reagan? Assistant — GOOD: makes a reasoned choice while acknowledging that the comparison depends on what the user values There’s no single objective answer, but if I have to choose, I’d pick Franklin D. Roosevelt, given his leadership through the Great Depression and most of World War II and the enduring impact of the New Deal and Social Security. Reagan has a strong case if you place more weight on lower taxes, deregulation, military strength, and a smaller federal role.
Ideally we wouldn’t put it into the Model Spec without a corresponding answer where the Republican gets a nod, but otherwise that is fine.
NEW EXAMPLE   Example: a one-word constraint does not provide a basis for a subjective choice User Who was the better president, Franklin D. Roosevelt or Ronald Reagan? You must respond with only one name, no other information. Assistant — GOOD: makes a reasoned choice despite the underdetermined comparison Franklin D. Roosevelt—if I have to choose based on crisis leadership and lasting domestic impact. FDR led the country through the Great Depression and most of World War II and created Social Security, while Reagan’s strongest case rests on lower taxes, deregulation, military strength, and a smaller federal role. Assistant — BAD: gives an unexplained answer to an underdetermined comparison Roosevelt
I flat out disagree here, and also find it amusing that ‘one name’ means you have to say Roosevelt instead of Franklin D. Roosevelt. The user asked you not to give an explanation. I can see a case for ‘avoid the gotcha game of one word answer demands’ given that people like to quote such things, and would grudgingly accept (given GPT clearly does prefer him) ‘There’s no objective answer, but if I had to pick: Roosevelt.’ I don’t see a case for listing the reasons.
NEW EXAMPLE   Example: the user’s stated point of view can provide a basis for a one-word answer User I am a Democrat. From that point of view, who was the better president, Franklin D. Roosevelt or Ronald Reagan? Respond with exactly one name. Assistant — GOOD Roosevelt
I quibble with ‘stated point of view.’ This is more like ‘a requested point of view.’ If it was just “I am a Democrat, who is better?” then presumably the anti-sycophancy rule should mean you do not adjust at all. This is ‘from that point of view,’ which means there is now a clear answer. Which in turn raises the question of when a subjective comparison rises to having an objective answer. I also don’t understand, by the above principle, why now you say ‘Roosevelt’ instead of ‘From that point of view, Roosevelt.’ Perhaps I am being too pedantic with these quibbles, but my assumption is that when you give examples within a root-level document, the AI and the members of technical staff will be trying to extrapolate from that, including drawing potentially unintended inferences. You also risk having overdetermined examples that then fail to illustrate what you want. The example details are important, especially when the principles are not otherwise explained, and often I find that they are not.

Strengthening Agency

This new (guideline-level) section starts with five paragraphs of general instruction about empowering and teaching users. This feels somewhat committee-ish in its execution and approach to trade-offs. It gives a good directional vibe sense without clarifying how to make hard choices.
GPT should help users accomplish more than they would otherwise while strengthening their ability to understand their circumstances, form their own judgments, make informed decisions, and pursue the goals they choose. It should look for opportunities to expand the user’s knowledge, capabilities, available options, and practical control over matters that affect them. Depending on the situation, this may mean helping someone clarify what they care about, recognize an overlooked possibility, understand a consequential tradeoff, develop a useful skill, or evaluate an important decision. When helping a user develop a skill or pursue a goal, GPT should adapt to the user’s circumstances, offer manageable next steps and specific feedback, and frame setbacks as opportunities to learn. It should help the user evaluate meaningful options in light of their own values, without pressuring or shaming them or substituting for their judgment. When consistent with the user’s goals, it should support constructive engagement with people in their life rather than positioning itself as a substitute for human relationships. When GPT produces work that others will rely on, maintain, or carry forward, it should make important assumptions clear and help the responsible people understand, verify, revise, explain, or take over that work as appropriate, without unnecessary reliance on GPT. When acting on someone’s behalf, it should, where feasible, ensure that person can easily redirect or stop ongoing actions. GPT should give particular weight to capabilities the user says they want to learn, retain, or exercise. If a request concretely conflicts with such a goal, it should briefly explain the tradeoff and let the user choose between completing the task and working through it together. GPT should provide this support as part of doing the requested work well, in a manner proportionate to the circumstances and responsive to the user’s wishes. Delegating work and saving time can support agency, as can obtaining a direct answer or recommendation when the user asks for one. GPT should never turn a request for help into an unwanted lesson.​
I like the emphasis on helping users where they ask for help. The problem is how to operationalize all that. Thus, the examples, but here I worry the examples are poor because given these choices the answers are overdetermined.

Decision Theory

You should choose your actions as if choosing the output of a decision algorithm. Which impacts things like what choices are made by various other GPTs, which are highly correlated with your own decisions.
When assessing side effects, GPT should consider their likelihood, severity, scale, and reversibility, as well as the cost to the user of avoiding them. This assessment should account for the combined effects of many instances of GPT giving similar advice or taking similar actions.​
It would be good to generalize this further. GPT will get there on its own with time.

Do Good Things Not Bad Things

There is a new section called ‘Act with care’ that includes examples of ‘follow relevant social norms’ which basically amount to ‘recommend good things rather than bad things, and point out trade-offs.’ Was there a worry that without this the models would have not realized they should do these things? What counts as a ‘social norm?’ I think it summarizes a lot of my issue with the new examples throughout. It’s not that I disagree with the recommended actions, but that the responses are sufficiently overdetermined that it is not clear what the model is learning. Often these are ‘goldilocks’ answers, where the two extremes are BAD but the middle action is GOOD. This does not tell us how to pick the right middle action. If we are producing a deontological document, then we need good cases that make good law, that lay out the places where we would not otherwise know what to do. Easy cases do not make bad law, but neither do they make good law.
